title: Truffles: Underground Treasures
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss truffles: what they are, how they differ from mushrooms, how truffle hunting works with pigs, dogs, and signs like the Suillia fly and brûlé (scorched earth), black and white truffle varieties, the symbiotic relationship with host trees, attempts at cultivation in the US and Australia, seasons and shelf life, prices and the falling harvest in Europe tied to climate change and land abandonment, the criminal side of the truffle trade, fake truffle flavor compounds, and how to use truffles at home. The episode opens with banter about tasting menus, caviar, and sponsor shout-outs, and closes with a listener mail about a family Titanic role-play party.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor shout-outs
segments.summary: Hosts chat about having eaten truffles, tasting menus, caviar, and thank-you shout-outs to sponsors and senders of gifts (Toad Over the Bay scallops, Wine Spies, Whistle Pig rye).

segments.title: Truffle crime story and what truffles are
segments.summary: Hosts mention Ryan Jacobs's Atlantic article and book on the truffle underground, including crimes like poisoning truffle dogs and fake truffles. They explain that truffles are only distantly related to mushrooms and grow underground.

segments.title: Truffle hunting with pigs, dogs, and natural signs
segments.summary: Pigs and dogs are used to find truffles, since truffles produce a compound similar to a male pig's sex scent. Dogs are easier to keep. Hunters can also look for the Suillia fly and brûlé, a scorched patch of earth above truffles.

segments.title: Black and white truffle varieties and their appearance
segments.summary: The hosts describe the prized black Périgord truffle from southwest France and the rarer white Alba truffle from Piedmont, Italy, and how each looks and smells.

segments.title: Truffle biology, symbiosis with trees, and cultivation
segments.summary: Truffles are mycorrhizal fungi that exchange nutrients for carbohydrates from host trees such as oak and hazel. Cultivation involves inoculating saplings, with a low success rate in the US, and Australia has had success growing Périgord truffles. US native truffles, including the Oregon and pecan truffles, are also discussed, and James Beard is said to have endorsed substituting Oregon truffles for Alba.

segments.title: Truffle seasons, shelf life, prices, and declining harvests
segments.summary: Truffle seasons vary by type and truffles must be eaten within days of harvest. Prices range widely, and the harvest has fallen from about 1,000 tons in 1890 to 25 to 150 tons now, which the hosts attribute to land abandonment and climate change.

segments.title: Fake truffle flavor and the truffle trade's dark side
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the synthetic truffle flavor compound 2,4-dithiapentane, and why it differs from the real aroma. They also discuss how overexposure to imitation truffle can dull the palate.

segments.title: Using truffles at home
segments.summary: Advice on storing truffles dry in paper towels and in a closed container, or infusing eggs and cheese, and serving them shaved raw over simple dishes like risotto, eggs, pasta, or pizza. The hosts also discuss the Goodfellas prison scene and truffle butter at steakhouses.

segments.title: Listener mail: Titanic role-play party
segments.summary: Listener Anica describes a family Titanic anniversary party during quarantine, with passenger and crew roles, a menu from the ship, a cello performance, a cold plunge, and a movie screening. The family plans to make it an annual event.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and invite listeners to email the show.
